widow.exampleMsg: Example loaded: a made-up couple who married in May 1777; his service ended in March 1778. The results are in the table below.
summary: Fits: the March 1855 bounty-land and 1878 laws (every rule checked here; other terms not checked)
Ruled out: the 1838, 1853 and February 1855 laws (by the dates)
Still possible: the 1836 and 1848 laws (need his kind of service)
Next: tell us his kind of service (Continental Line, or State troops, volunteers or militia); then look for the widow's pension file (see "What to do next").

rows.verdict: Still possible: need his kind of service
rows.rule: Rule: Marriage must precede expiration of veteran's last period of service; service as specified in act of June 7, 1832 (at least 6 months, in the Continental Line or State troops, volunteers or militia).To settle it, tell us his kind of service (Continental Line, or State troops, volunteers or militia).Not checked here (from the law's own text): She was paid only while she stayed unmarried.What to do: find out what kind of unit he served in. For state militia, the National Archives says to check the archives of the state where he served; for Continental troops, see its service-records guide.National Archives: Revolutionary War service records (PDF) (opens in new tab)Read the 1836 law itself: 5 Stat. 128 (Library of Congress scan, large PDF, about 23 MB; opens at the law's page in most browsers) (opens in new tab)

Rule: Service as specified in act of June 7, 1832 (at least 6 months, in the Continental Line or State troops, volunteers or militia); marriage after his last period of service ended and before January 1, 1794.No action needed for this law: what you typed already rules it out. If something you typed is wrong, fix it and check again.

rows.law: Act of July 29, 1848 (9 Stat. 265) — life pensions
rows.verdict: Still possible: need his kind of service
rows.rule: Rule: Marriage before January 2, 1800; he served in the Continental line, State troops, volunteers, militia or the naval service.To settle it, tell us his kind of service (Continental Line, or State troops, volunteers or militia).Not checked here (from the law's own text): It was paid during her widowhood. A widow already receiving a pension could not get a further one under this law.What to do: find out what kind of unit he served in. For state militia, the National Archives says to check the archives of the state where he served; for Continental troops, see its service-records guide.National Archives: Revolutionary War service records (PDF) (opens in new tab)Read the 1848 law itself: 9 Stat. 265 (Library of Congress scan, large PDF, about 19 MB; opens at the law's page in most browsers) (opens in new tab)

Rule: Widow of an officer or soldier of the Revolutionary army, married after January 1800.No action needed for this law: what you typed already rules it out. If something you typed is wrong, fix it and check again.

Rule: Widow of a navy officer, marine or mariner of the Revolutionary War, married since January 1, 1800.No action needed for this law: what you typed already rules it out. If something you typed is wrong, fix it and check again.

rows.law: Bounty-land act of March 3, 1855 (10 Stat. 701) — 160 acres
rows.verdict: Fits the rules checked here; other terms not checked
rows.rule: Rule: At least 14 days of service, or actually in a battle; the law extended to Revolutionary War soldiers, their widows and minor children.Not checked here (from the law's own text): Militia, volunteers or State troops had to have been regularly mustered, with the service paid by the United States. No warrant if the muster rolls show he deserted or was dishonorably discharged. A widow who had married again could still apply if she was a widow when she applied.Read the 1855 bounty-land law itself: 10 Stat. 701 (Library of Congress scan, large PDF, about 89 MB; opens at the law's page in most browsers) (opens in new tab)

rows.law: Act of March 9, 1878 (20 Stat. 29) — widows' life pensions
rows.verdict: Fits the rules checked here; other terms not checked
rows.rule: Rule: A widow of a Revolutionary soldier who served at least 14 days or was in any engagement.Not checked here (from the law's own text): Her pension ended if she married again. It didn't apply to anyone already receiving a pension of $8 a month or more.Read the 1878 law itself: 20 Stat. 27 (Library of Congress scan, large PDF, about 88 MB; opens at the law's page in most browsers) (opens in new tab)

plan: Answer one more question Tell us his kind of service (Continental Line, or State troops, volunteers or militia), in the "What kind of service was it?" box, then check again. It bears on the 1836 and 1848 laws.

Look for the widow's pension file Widows' pension files are marked with a W and a file number. A widow's application may give her age, residence, maiden name, the date and place of the marriage, and the date and place of her husband's death, so it can prove a marriage in your line. The files are online free on FamilySearch (login needed). You can also order a copy of a Revolutionary War pension file from the National Archives with its NATF Form 85. where: A. Look for a death certificate. DAR: the most common record types for proving a line (opens in new tab) Our guide: No Birth Certificate? Substitute Evidence For: Gen 2 death

B. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds state death certificates for 1906 to 1975, and all certified copies of death records come from the Department of Health's Division of Vital Records. Pennsylvania Department of Health: vital records for genealogy (opens in new tab) Pennsylvania State Archives: archival birth and death certificates (opens in new tab) For: Gen 2 death

C. Look for a long-form birth certificate that names the parents; short forms without the parents' names don't count. The 1880–1900 censuses are also listed as a source. DAR: the most common record types for proving a line (opens in new tab) Our guide: No Birth Certificate? Substitute Evidence Our guide: From the 1850 Census Back to 1776 For: Gen 2 parent–child link; Gen 3 parent–child link

D. Look for a long-form birth certificate (the kind that names the parents). No certificate? A baptism or christening record can stand in for the birth date. DAR: the most common record types for proving a line (opens in new tab) Our guide: No Birth Certificate? Substitute Evidence For: Gen 3 birth
E. Virginia counties and cities kept birth registers from 1853 to 1896. Library of Virginia: birth, marriage and death records (1853 to present) (opens in new tab) For: Gen 3 birth
F. Census: NSCDA lists the 1880–1900 censuses as primary sources. For: Gen 3 birth; Gen 3 parent–child link; Gen 4 birth or death

G. Look for a church baptism record. An age given in a census or at death can be used to estimate a birth year. H. Virginia had no statewide recording of births before 1853, so there is no state birth record to find for this person. Birth records from before then are rare. How to prove a birth without a birth certificate (our guide) Library of Virginia: birth, marriage and death records (1853 to present) (opens in new tab) For: Gen 4 birth or death; Gen 5 birth or death
I. Census: The 1790–1840 censuses named only the head of household and counted everyone else by age group. For: Gen 4 birth or death; Gen 5 birth or death
J. Census: The 1850–1870 censuses do not state relationships. For: Gen 4 birth or death
plan: Prove the patriot's service Where to look, based on the type of service and the state served for: The National Archives does not hold state militia records; check that state's archives. The 1832 pension law opened pensions to militia service of at least six months, so look for a pension file too. DAR also asks for original records such as pensions, muster rolls and pay vouchers. Virginia: Most Virginians who served did so in the county militia, and the Library of Virginia says few records of militia service exist. Militia officer appointments are often in the county court order books, and many federal pensions after 1832 mention militia service. Payrolls and muster rolls exist for most Continental Line soldiers. SAR does not take family tradition as proof of service. Check the widow-pension laws for your patriot Widows could apply for pensions from 1836. A widow's application may give her maiden name and the date and place of the marriage, so her file can prove a link in your line. The free checker shows which widow laws fit; it can fill in the service end date from this worksheet. Widow Pension Law Checker (free tool on this site) Guide: How to Read a Revolutionary War Pension File
